source.title: Neumann Optimizer: A Practical Optimization Algorithm for Deep Neural Networks
source.authors: Shankar Krishnan; Ying Xiao; Rif A. Saurous

record.tranche_reason: The study varies batch size and optimizer on natural image classification and reports validation error, refining the claim about large-batch generalization by showing that a new optimizer preserves or improves validation performance at large batch sizes.
record.gate_note: Reports its own optimizer, batch-size, regularization-ablation, and optimizer-comparison results on ImageNet. It also reports a CIFAR-10 Hessian-eigenvalue measurement; that property is not a versioned measure of the training–test gap. Cited findings about other optimizers and large-batch training are not rows.
record.test_reason: The batch-size sweep and epoch-indexed validation curves bear on V5 using a new optimizer. However, the tabulated endpoints use different epoch budgets, so they do not establish the fixed-epoch penalty or its removal. The optimizer comparisons do not test V4's adaptive-method-versus-SGD comparison.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes the authors' conclusion: Neumann handles batches up to 32000 while matching or improving baseline validation quality, and improves smaller-batch validation error by about 0.8–0.9 percentage points without improving classification loss. Their baseline-relative statement does not mean accuracy remains constant across Neumann batch sizes.
record.recipe_differences: Introduces a Neumann-series optimizer with cubic and repulsive regularizers, SGD warm-up, and a scheduled learning rate; compares it with RMSProp and SGD with momentum. It does not reproduce the original methods in V4 or V5.
record.method_sensitivity: Mini-batch size changes validation error; removing the optimizer's cubic and repulsive regularizers worsens it. Tacotron with aggressive gradient clipping did not gain speed or quality.

fits_no_version.finding: Neumann improves ImageNet validation error over RMSProp or momentum SGD; Adam is worse than RMSProp and Neumann in the reported comparison.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimizer choice affects ImageNet validation performance, with Neumann outperforming the tested baseline recipes.

fits_no_version.finding: At batch 4000, Neumann's cubic and repulsive regularizers reduce validation error from 23.5% to 23.0%; the baseline is 24.3%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The proposed optimizer's internal regularizers improve its validation performance in this setting.

fits_no_version.finding: During SGD on CIFAR-10, the largest mini-batch Hessian eigenvalue rises while the most negative approaches zero.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Extremal mini-batch Hessian eigenvalues change systematically during the studied training trajectory.

fits_no_version.finding: Neumann provides no reported speed or quality improvement on Tacotron with aggressive gradient clipping.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Neumann's benefits do not extend to the tested speech-synthesis training setup.

record.code_released: The authors say they intend to open source the code at a later date; no URL is stated.
record.problems: Results are from single runs throughout the experimental section; no run-to-run uncertainty estimates are reported. The study reports ImageNet results, while CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 experiments are not reported. Large-batch comparisons use Neumann optimizer and a selected schedule rather than an across-optimizer fixed-epoch comparison.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible result rows omitted. The CIFAR-10 Hessian eigenvalue figure is not a measure of the training–test gap, so it is described under fits_no_version rather than extracted as a version row.

untested.parts: Random-label memorization and corresponding natural-label and random-label held-out accuracy.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and local connectivity.
Adaptive gradient methods versus SGD under limited or broader tuning, optimizer switching, decoupled weight decay, and word-level language modeling.
Matched fixed-epoch endpoint comparisons are not tabulated; language models and separate causal tests of longer training, learning-rate scaling, warmup, and normalization are absent.
Dropout and joint removal of dropout and weight decay.
Magnitude-scaled perturbation tolerance, generalization gaps, and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing memorized versus random training examples.

missing.what: Validation-error comparisons at common epoch counts for Neumann batches 1600, 16000, and 32000 and the momentum-SGD baseline at batch 1600. These curves directly address the fixed-budget question, unlike Table 3's unequal-duration endpoints. The supplied text does not preserve readable curve values, so no directional verdict is assigned.

record.verdict_notes: No version-specific verdict is justified by the extracted endpoints: the V4 comparator is mismatched, and V5 requires matched epoch budgets. Experimental results are generally single runs, although Appendix C shows two Inception-V3 runs with similar final quality.

versions.untested_parts: Memorization of random labels and generalization on natural labels.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons.
The comparisons cover the tested image classifiers only; no language benchmark or broad optimizer tuning comparison is reported.
The study does not compare large and small batches at a fixed epoch budget across image classifiers and language models, and does not test all the adaptation methods listed in the version.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to generalization gaps.

rows.subject: Adam
rows.operation_detail: Compared Adam with Neumann optimizer and RMSProp on Inception-V3.
rows.measure: Top-1 validation error; described as substantially inferior to both comparators.
rows.baseline: Neumann optimizer and RMSProp; exact values not assigned to Adam in the table.
rows.value: substantially inferior performance compared to both Neumann optimizer and RMSProp
rows.note: The authors report qualitative comparison; the figure's Adam curve is not transcribed into a numerical value.
rows.check: Adam performs worse than RMSProp and Neumann here; neither comparator establishes V4's comparison with SGD. Inferiority is explicitly reported, rather than partial, but it does not measure a versioned effect.

rows.subject: Inception-V3
rows.operation_detail: Trained with Neumann optimizer versus the baseline RMSProp recipe.
rows.note: Authors report a 0.91% improvement; classification loss was not improved.
rows.check: Neumann versus RMSProp measures the proposed optimizer's performance, not adaptive methods versus SGD. Batch size 64 is per GPU; synchronous training uses 50 GPUs.

rows.subject: Resnet-50
rows.operation_detail: Trained with Neumann optimizer versus the baseline SGD with momentum recipe.

conditions.value: Neumann versus baseline SGD with momentum

rows.check: Neumann versus momentum SGD does not establish the behavior of the adaptive gradient methods named in V4. Batch size 32 is per GPU in the 50-GPU setup.

rows.subject: Resnet-101
rows.operation_detail: Trained with Neumann optimizer versus the baseline SGD with momentum recipe.

conditions.value: Neumann versus baseline SGD with momentum

rows.check: Neumann versus momentum SGD measures the proposed optimizer's performance, not V4's adaptive gradient comparison. Batch size 32 is per GPU.

rows.subject: Inception-Resnet-V2
rows.operation_detail: Trained with Neumann optimizer versus the baseline RMSProp recipe.
rows.check: Neumann versus RMSProp lacks an SGD comparator. Batch size 64 is per GPU; synchronous training uses 50 GPUs.

rows.subject: Resnet-50
rows.operation_detail: Trained with Neumann optimizer at varying mini-batch sizes using the Section 4.1 learning-rate schedule.
rows.note: The study gives no corresponding fixed-epoch small-batch comparison in this table.
rows.check: This is the reference condition, not evidence of a batch-size penalty. Its endpoint is 23.0% after 226 epochs; comparing the row with itself cannot establish V5.

rows.subject: Resnet-50
rows.operation_detail: Trained with Neumann optimizer at varying mini-batch sizes using the Section 4.1 learning-rate schedule.
rows.note: Authors report that the optimizer remains better than the baseline; epoch counts are also reported but are not a generalization-gap measure.
rows.check: The equal 23.0% endpoint uses 230 epochs versus 226 for batch 1600. It does not establish absence of a penalty at a fixed epoch budget.

rows.subject: Resnet-50
rows.operation_detail: Trained with Neumann optimizer at varying mini-batch sizes using the Section 4.1 learning-rate schedule.
rows.note: The error is slightly higher than the 1600-batch result; authors state all tested sizes remain better than the baseline.
rows.check: The 23.1% endpoint uses 258 epochs versus 226 for the reference. The 0.1 percentage-point difference cannot isolate the fixed-epoch batch-size effect.

rows.subject: Resnet-50
rows.operation_detail: Trained with Neumann optimizer at varying mini-batch sizes using the Section 4.1 learning-rate schedule.
rows.note: The error rises relative to batch size 1600 but remains below the 24.3% baseline cited in Section 4.3 for a batch size of 4000; those baselines are not identical conditions.
rows.check: The 23.5% endpoint uses 210 epochs versus 226 for the reference. The endpoint difference confounds batch size and training duration.

rows.subject: Resnet-50
rows.operation_detail: Trained with Neumann optimizer at varying mini-batch sizes using the Section 4.1 learning-rate schedule.
rows.note: The authors state this is still better than the baseline, while validation error increases compared with the 1600-batch result.
rows.check: The 24.0% endpoint uses 237 epochs versus 226 for the reference. It shows worse final accuracy, but does not establish V5's fixed-epoch effect.

rows.subject: Resnet-50
rows.operation_detail: Compared Neumann optimizer with and without its cubic and repulsive regularizer terms at batch size 4000.
rows.note: The table tests the optimizer's internal regularizers, not dropout or weight decay. Baseline recipe detail is not restated in this section.
rows.check: This compares optimizers and internal regularization at one batch size. It establishes neither adaptive methods versus SGD nor a large-versus-small batch effect.

rows.subject: Resnet-50
rows.operation_detail: Compared Neumann optimizer without its cubic and repulsive regularizer terms against the baseline.
rows.note: Authors state that regularization improves validation performance, but performance without it still improves over baseline.
rows.check: The internal regularizer ablation does not measure V4 or V5. Its regularizers are neither dropout nor the dropout-and-weight-decay removal named in V6.

rows.subject: Resnet-50
rows.operation_detail: Compared a Neumann-trained model at batch size 32000 with the baseline in the text.
rows.locator: Section 4.2, text accompanying Figure 3 and Table 3
rows.note: Qualitative statement about the baseline; retained separately from the table's batch-size comparison.
rows.check: This duplicates R10's result with a different comparator. Figure 3 identifies the baseline as momentum SGD at batch 1600; the qualitative endpoint comparison does not specify a matched epoch budget.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.reason: Neumann improves reported validation error over the tested baselines, while Adam is described as substantially worse than RMSProp and Neumann; this is a different optimizer and tuning comparison from the version's adaptive-method examples (R1–R5, R11–R12).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Resnet-50 on ImageNet with Neumann optimizer and the reported learning-rate schedule
reader_labels.reason: Up to batch size 32000, the authors say quality remains better than baseline, but validation error rises from 23.0 % at batch size 1600 to 24.0 % at batch size 32000; the tested setup does not establish a fixed-epoch large-versus-small batch penalty (R6–R10, R13).
